subtopic_detail: Acute haematogenous osteomyelitis versus septic arthritis in a school aged child
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar in a regional emergency department. A 7 year old boy has been limping for four days and since yesterday will not put any weight on his left leg. His mother says he has been hot and off his food, and that he has not had any fall or twisting injury.

He holds the leg still but allows you to move the knee through a full range without resisting, and there is no swelling or warmth over the joint line. There is sharply localised tenderness over the bone just above the knee. A plain radiograph of the femur and knee is reported as normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 128, blood pressure 98/60, respiratory rate 24, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 38.7
data_table.Examination: Point tenderness over the distal femoral metaphysis, full passive knee range with no effusion, no rash
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 14.2 x10^9/L (5.0-15.0); C-reactive protein 88 mg/L (less than 5); two sets of blood cultures taken

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Aspirate the left knee under sedation and send fluid for urgent culture
options.rationale: Joint aspiration is the priority when the joint itself is infected, but a full painless passive range with no effusion argues strongly against septic arthritis and aspirating a normal joint delays treatment of the bone (Source: RCH CPG: Acute Osteomyelitis and Septic Arthritis).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Acute Osteomyelitis and Septic Arthritis

options.text: Start oral cefalexin and review in the outpatient clinic in 48 hours
options.rationale: Oral therapy is used only after clinical and biochemical improvement on intravenous treatment, and cefalexin is the step down agent rather than the initial choice in a febrile child who cannot weight bear (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Start intravenous flucloxacillin and arrange magnetic resonance imaging
options.rationale: Staphylococcus aureus is the dominant pathogen so empirical intravenous flucloxacillin is started once cultures are drawn, and magnetic resonance imaging is the imaging of choice because plain films stay normal for the first ten to fourteen days (Source: RCH CPG: Acute Osteomyelitis and Septic Arthritis; Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Acute Osteomyelitis and Septic Arthritis

options.text: Repeat the plain radiograph in seven days and withhold antibiotics now
options.rationale: Waiting for radiographic periosteal reaction risks growth plate damage and chronic infection, since the changes lag the illness by one to two weeks (Source: RCH CPG: Acute Osteomyelitis and Septic Arthritis).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Acute Osteomyelitis and Septic Arthritis

options.text: Arrange a technetium bone scan before starting antimicrobial therapy
options.rationale: Bone scan is reserved for multifocal disease or when the site is unclear, and it is less specific than magnetic resonance imaging while adding radiation and delay (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Osteomyelitis in Children).
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Osteomyelitis in Children

explanation.summary: Acute haematogenous osteomyelitis in children seeds the metaphysis of a long bone, most often around the knee, because of the sluggish flow in the metaphyseal sinusoids. The clinical separation from septic arthritis rests on whether passive joint movement is preserved, since a child with pus in the joint resists any movement at all. Blood cultures are positive in roughly half of cases and are the only microbiological sample obtained in most children, so they must be taken before the first dose. Magnetic resonance imaging detects marrow oedema within days and also demonstrates subperiosteal collections that need surgical drainage.
key_points: Preserved painless passive joint range points to bone rather than joint infection
Plain radiographs remain normal for ten to fourteen days and never exclude the diagnosis
Take blood cultures before the first intravenous antibiotic dose
Empirical cover targets Staphylococcus aureus with intravenous flucloxacillin
Magnetic resonance imaging identifies collections requiring surgical drainage
explanation.pearls: In a child under 5 years who is not fully immunised against Haemophilus influenzae type b, add a third generation cephalosporin to flucloxacillin until cultures return at 48 hours.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Acute Osteomyelitis and Septic Arthritis
BMJ Best Practice: Osteomyelitis in Children

subtopic_detail: Distinguishing an innocent murmur from pathology at a routine child health check
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 4 year old boy for his routine health check. His mother mentions that he seemed puffed at a swimming lesson last month, although he keeps up with his older sister in the backyard and has never gone blue or floppy.

He was born at term and his growth has tracked along the 50th centile for height and weight. You hear a soft systolic murmur at the left lower sternal edge with a musical vibratory quality. It becomes much quieter when he stands, the second heart sound splits normally with respiration, and femoral pulses are equal and easily felt. There is no thrill and no radiation to the back or neck.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 96, blood pressure 96/58, respiratory rate 22, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.6
data_table.Examination: Grade 2 of 6 vibratory systolic murmur at the left lower sternal edge, quieter on standing, no hepatomegaly
data_table.Investigations: Growth parameters on the 50th centile, no previous cardiac investigations

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Reassure the parents and review the murmur at the next health check
options.rationale: A soft vibratory systolic murmur that varies with posture, with a normally split second sound, palpable femoral pulses and normal growth, meets every feature of a Still murmur and needs no investigation (Source: RCH CPG: Heart Murmurs).

options.text: Refer for transthoracic echocardiography before any further review
options.rationale: Echocardiography is indicated when any red flag is present, such as a diastolic or pansystolic murmur, a thrill, an abnormal second sound or absent femoral pulses, none of which he has (Source: RCH CPG: Heart Murmurs).

options.text: Arrange an electrocardiogram and chest radiograph at the local hospital
options.rationale: Both tests have poor sensitivity and specificity for structural disease in this setting, and a normal result would not change the assessment already made at the bedside (Source: RCH CPG: Heart Murmurs).

options.text: Refer urgently to paediatric cardiology for review within one week
options.rationale: Urgent referral is reserved for cyanosis, failure to thrive, syncope on exertion or a murmur in an infant under 12 months, and being briefly puffed during a swimming lesson does not qualify (Source: RCH CPG: Heart Murmurs).

options.text: Commence antibiotic prophylaxis before any future dental procedures
options.rationale: Prophylaxis is restricted to defined high risk lesions such as prosthetic valves, prior endocarditis and rheumatic heart disease, and an innocent murmur confers no risk at all (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

explanation.summary: Up to half of all healthy children have an audible murmur at some point, and the great majority are innocent flow murmurs of which the Still murmur is the commonest. The clinical task is to apply a short list of red flags rather than to investigate every murmur, because unnecessary echocardiography generates anxiety and cost without changing outcomes. Postural variation is the single most useful bedside manoeuvre, since innocent murmurs soften markedly when preload falls on standing while pathological murmurs generally do not. Femoral pulse palpation is mandatory at every murmur assessment because coarctation can present with a soft murmur and normal growth in early childhood.
key_points: Still murmur is soft, vibratory, at the left lower sternal edge, and softens on standing
Red flags are diastolic timing, pansystolic timing, a thrill, an abnormal second sound or weak femoral pulses
Any murmur in an infant under 12 months warrants cardiology assessment
Electrocardiogram and chest radiograph do not usefully triage a childhood murmur
Endocarditis prophylaxis applies only to defined high risk cardiac lesions
explanation.pearls: A venous hum is continuous, loudest under the right clavicle when sitting, and abolished by turning the head or gently compressing the ipsilateral internal jugular vein, which instantly distinguishes it from a patent ductus arteriosus.

subtopic_detail: Imaging versus structured observation after minor head injury in a toddler
stem:
You are the emergency department resident assessing an 18 month old girl who rolled off a kitchen bench while her father was changing her, falling about 1.5 metres onto tiles two hours ago. She cried immediately, was never floppy or unresponsive, and her father says she is behaving completely normally now and has taken a full bottle without vomiting.

She is alert, tracks you around the cubicle and reaches for her toy. There is a boggy swelling over the right parietal region about 4 cm across. The anterior fontanelle is closed, the pupils are equal and reactive, and she moves all four limbs symmetrically.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 128, blood pressure 94/56, respiratory rate 28, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.8
data_table.Examination: Glasgow coma scale 15, boggy right parietal haematoma 4 cm, no palpable step, no bruising behind the ears

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Perform an immediate computed tomography scan of her brain
options.rationale: Immediate imaging is reserved for high risk features such as a Glasgow coma scale below 15, a suspected depressed or basal skull fracture, seizure or focal deficit, none of which are present (Source: RCH CPG: Head Injury).

options.text: Discharge now with written head injury advice for the parents
options.rationale: A non frontal scalp haematoma in a child under 2 years combined with a fall over 0.9 metres places her in the intermediate risk group, where immediate discharge misses the small number of clinically important injuries (Source: RCH CPG: Head Injury).

options.text: Arrange a skull radiograph to exclude an underlying linear fracture
options.rationale: Skull radiography has no role in the modern paediatric head injury pathway because a fracture may be absent with significant intracranial injury and present without it (Source: RCH CPG: Head Injury).

options.text: Admit her for magnetic resonance imaging of the brain in the morning
options.rationale: Magnetic resonance imaging is not the acute test for traumatic haemorrhage and usually requires sedation at this age, so it neither answers the urgent question nor is available in time (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Paediatric Head Injury).
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Paediatric Head Injury

options.text: Observe with hourly neurological observations for at least four hours
options.rationale: Intermediate risk children are managed with a structured period of observation of at least four hours from the injury, with imaging only if the conscious state, vomiting or headache deteriorates (Source: RCH CPG: Head Injury; PREDICT Australian and New Zealand Head Injury Guideline).
source_refs: PREDICT Australian and New Zealand Head Injury Guideline

explanation.summary: The Australian and New Zealand paediatric head injury guideline uses a three tier structure of high, intermediate and low risk, with observation as the deliberate middle path rather than a compromise. In children under 2 years the predictors differ from older children, and a non frontal scalp haematoma carries real weight because the skull is thin and the history of loss of consciousness is unreliable. Observation is safe because clinically important traumatic brain injury almost always declares itself with deteriorating conscious state, persistent vomiting or increasing irritability within the first hours. Choosing observation over scanning avoids an ionising radiation dose to a developing brain in a group where the yield is around one per cent.
key_points: Under 2 years, a non frontal scalp haematoma is a risk factor in its own right
A fall over 0.9 metres counts as a severe mechanism in this age group
Observation runs for at least four hours from the time of injury, not from arrival
Skull radiographs have no place in the pathway
Deterioration during observation converts the plan to computed tomography
explanation.pearls: Vomiting alone after a paediatric head injury is a weak predictor and does not mandate a scan, but three or more episodes or vomiting that starts more than four hours after the injury should trigger imaging.

sources.label: PREDICT Australian and New Zealand Head Injury Guideline
BMJ Best Practice: Paediatric Head Injury

subtopic_detail: First hour management of a suspected snake bite in a rural child
stem:
You are the sole doctor at a small rural Victorian hospital. A 9 year old boy is brought in 40 minutes after he felt a sharp scratch on his ankle while walking through long dry grass and saw a snake move away. His father applied a broad elasticised bandage firmly from the foot upwards over the whole leg and splinted it before driving him in.

The boy is alert and talking, says his leg feels tight but not painful, and has not vomited. There is no bleeding from the bandage edge and no swelling of the visible toes. The bandage is intact and correctly applied. Your hospital stocks antivenom and has a laboratory on site.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 96, blood pressure 108/64, respiratory rate 20, SpO2 100 per cent on room air, temperature 36.5
data_table.Examination: Pressure immobilisation bandage and splint in place over the left leg, no ptosis, no tender lymph nodes, power and speech normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Remove the bandage now and observe closely for local swelling
options.rationale: The bandage stays on until the child is in a facility able to treat envenoming and baseline bloods are back, because removal releases venom into the systemic circulation (Source: RCH CPG: Snakebite).

options.text: Leave the bandage in place and take coagulation studies and creatine kinase
options.rationale: Australian envenoming is diagnosed biochemically, so a baseline international normalised ratio, activated partial thromboplastin time, D dimer, full blood count, electrolytes and creatine kinase are taken with the bandage undisturbed and repeated serially (Source: RCH CPG: Snakebite; Australian Snakebite Project consensus guidelines).

options.text: Give one vial of polyvalent antivenom before any blood tests are taken
options.rationale: Antivenom is given only for proven or strongly suspected envenoming because of the risk of anaphylaxis, and most Australian snake bites deliver no venom at all (Source: RCH CPG: Snakebite).

options.text: Swab the bite site for a venom detection kit and await that result
options.rationale: The venom detection kit selects which monovalent antivenom to give once envenoming is established, and it never determines whether envenoming has occurred (Source: Australian Snakebite Project consensus guidelines).

options.text: Give intramuscular adrenaline and transfer to the nearest tertiary hospital
options.rationale: Adrenaline premedication is not routine and is given as treatment for anaphylaxis or alongside antivenom in specific circumstances, neither of which applies to a well child with no systemic features (Source: RCH CPG: Snakebite).

explanation.summary: Australian snake envenoming is defined by laboratory and clinical evidence of a venom effect rather than by the bite itself, and roughly three quarters of bites are dry. The pressure immobilisation bandage works by limiting lymphatic spread and is left undisturbed until the child is somewhere antivenom can be given safely and baseline results are available. Serial testing at baseline, one hour and six hours is the standard because venom induced consumption coagulopathy and myotoxicity can declare late. Discharge is only considered after twelve hours of observation with normal repeat bloods and neurological examination.
key_points: Most Australian snake bites are dry and do not need antivenom
Never remove the pressure immobilisation bandage before baseline bloods and antivenom access
Baseline and serial coagulation studies plus creatine kinase define envenoming
The venom detection kit chooses the antivenom, it does not diagnose envenoming
Observe for at least twelve hours with repeat testing before discharge
explanation.pearls: An undetectable fibrinogen with an unrecordable international normalised ratio indicates venom induced consumption coagulopathy from a brown or tiger snake, and it is corrected by antivenom rather than by fresh frozen plasma given first.

subtopic_detail: Retractile versus true undescended testis and the timing of referral
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing an 8 month old boy brought in by his father for a routine check. He was born at term and has grown along the 50th centile.

On a warm couch with relaxed legs, the right hemiscrotum is empty and flat. You can feel the right testis in the inguinal canal and can coax it down as far as the upper scrotum, but it springs back up as soon as you let go and will not sit in the scrotum. The left testis is normally sited and of equal size. The penis is normally formed with a terminal meatus, and the same right sided finding was documented at his 3 month check.

data_table.Examination: Right testis palpable in the inguinal canal, does not remain in the scrotum on release, left testis normally descended, no hernia

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Reassure that this is a retractile testis and review him at age two years
options.rationale: A retractile testis stays in the scrotum once brought down and only retracts with cremasteric stimulation, whereas this one springs straight back, which defines a true undescended testis (Source: RCH CPG: Undescended Testes).

options.text: Request an inguinal and scrotal ultrasound to locate the right testis
options.rationale: Ultrasound adds nothing when the testis is already palpable and its poor accuracy for an impalpable testis means it does not alter the surgical plan either (Source: RCH CPG: Undescended Testes).

options.text: Arrange a chorionic gonadotrophin stimulation test before any referral
options.rationale: Hormonal testing belongs to the workup of bilateral impalpable testes with possible disorders of sex development, not a unilateral palpable undescended testis in a normally virilised boy (Source: RCH CPG: Undescended Testes).

options.text: Refer to paediatric surgery now for operative correction before 12 months
options.rationale: Spontaneous descent effectively ceases after 6 months of corrected age, and orchidopexy between 6 and 12 months preserves germ cell numbers and reduces later malignancy and infertility risk (Source: RCH CPG: Undescended Testes; RACGP: Undescended Testes in Children).

options.text: Review him again in the general practice clinic at 18 months of age
options.rationale: Waiting until 18 months pushes surgery well past the window in which germ cell loss accelerates, and no further spontaneous descent is expected after 6 months (Source: RACGP: Undescended Testes in Children).

explanation.summary: Around three per cent of term boys have an undescended testis at birth and most descend spontaneously by 3 to 6 months, after which further descent is rare. The clinical separation from a retractile testis is entirely a bedside one and turns on whether the testis remains in the scrotum after being brought down. Early orchidopexy matters because germ cell degeneration begins in the first year and the risks of subfertility and testicular malignancy both rise with delay. An impalpable testis follows a different pathway, with examination under anaesthesia and diagnostic laparoscopy rather than imaging.
key_points: A retractile testis remains in the scrotum after being milked down, an undescended one does not
Spontaneous descent is not expected after 6 months of corrected age
Orchidopexy is timed between 6 and 12 months
Ultrasound has no role in the palpable or the impalpable undescended testis
An impalpable testis goes to examination under anaesthesia and laparoscopy
explanation.pearls: Bilateral impalpable testes in a newborn is an endocrine emergency until congenital adrenal hyperplasia in a virilised female is excluded, so check electrolytes and 17 hydroxyprogesterone rather than booking elective surgery.

subtopic_detail: Persistent otitis media with effusion causing speech delay
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 3 year 6 month old boy whose parents say he turns the television up until the neighbours complain and often does not answer when called from another room. His childcare educator has raised that he uses only about thirty words and that strangers cannot understand him.

He has had frequent colds but has never had a painful discharging ear or a fever with ear pain. His parents first raised the hearing concern with you four months ago and the same findings were documented then. Otoscopy today shows dull retracted tympanic membranes bilaterally with a visible air fluid level and no erythema or bulging. Tympanometry gives a flat trace in both ears.

data_table.Examination: Bilateral dull retracted tympanic membranes with air fluid levels, no discharge, no cervical lymphadenopathy
data_table.Investigations: Type B flat tympanogram bilaterally, growth and developmental milestones otherwise age appropriate

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer for formal audiology and ear nose and throat assessment now
options.rationale: Effusion persisting beyond three months with hearing concern and speech delay is the threshold for formal audiological assessment and specialist referral for consideration of ventilation tubes (Source: RCH CPG: Otitis Media; Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Prescribe a two week course of oral amoxicillin and then review him
options.rationale: Antibiotics produce at best a small short lived reduction in effusion volume and no lasting hearing benefit, and there is no acute infection here to treat (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Start an intranasal corticosteroid spray and review in three months
options.rationale: Intranasal corticosteroids do not shorten the duration of middle ear effusion in children and using them would add another three months of unaddressed hearing loss (Source: Cochrane Review: Topical Steroids for Otitis Media with Effusion).
source_refs: Cochrane Review: Topical Steroids for Otitis Media with Effusion

options.text: Advise autoinflation with a nasal balloon and review him in six months
options.rationale: Autoinflation is a reasonable adjunct in older cooperative children with a shorter history, but it is not a substitute for audiology when speech development is already affected (Source: RCH CPG: Otitis Media).

options.text: Reassure that this resolves spontaneously and review him at age four
options.rationale: Watchful waiting is correct for the first three months in a child with normal language, but that window has closed once the effusion is documented over four months with a speech delay (Source: RCH CPG: Otitis Media).

explanation.summary: Otitis media with effusion is fluid in the middle ear without the signs of acute infection, and most episodes clear within three months without any treatment. The decision point is not the appearance of the drum but the functional consequence, so persistent bilateral effusion with a conductive hearing loss and delayed speech converts observation into referral. Australian practice adds a specific caution for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children, in whom effusion and suppurative disease are far more common and the threshold for audiology and specialist review is lower. Untreated conductive loss during the peak language acquisition years has effects on speech and school readiness that persist after the fluid clears.
key_points: Effusion under three months in a child with normal language is observed
Persistent bilateral effusion with speech delay warrants audiology and specialist referral
A flat type B tympanogram supports effusion but does not quantify the hearing loss
Antibiotics, antihistamines and decongestants do not change the natural history
Ventilation tubes are considered for persistent bilateral effusion with functional impact
explanation.pearls: A unilateral persistent middle ear effusion in an adolescent or adult, particularly of Southern Chinese or South East Asian background, needs nasopharyngeal examination to exclude a nasopharyngeal carcinoma obstructing the eustachian tube.

sources.label: Cochrane Review: Topical Steroids for Otitis Media with Effusion

subtopic_detail: Adrenaline autoinjector device banding after a first food reaction in infancy
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing an 11 month old girl two days after her first taste of scrambled egg. Her mother says that within ten minutes her lips puffed up, red itchy welts spread over her whole body, she vomited three times and went pale and floppy in her highchair for a minute or so before perking up after a dose of the antihistamine they had at home.

She has mild eczema controlled with a moisturiser and has tolerated dairy, wheat and peanut without any reaction. She is thriving and today is completely well with a normal examination. Her weight is 9.2 kg.

data_table.Examination: Weight 9.2 kg on the 50th centile, chest clear, skin shows mild flexural eczema only
data_table.Investigations: No allergy testing performed to date

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management to arrange today?

options.text: Prescribe a 300 microgram adrenaline autoinjector and refer to allergy
options.rationale: The 300 microgram device is banded for children weighing 20 kg or more, so it is the wrong strength for a 9.2 kg infant even though the referral component is right (Source: ASCIA Guidelines: Prescribing Adrenaline Autoinjectors).

options.text: Arrange skin prick testing first and defer any device prescription
options.rationale: Testing confirms sensitisation but the reaction has already met the definition of anaphylaxis, and delaying the device leaves her unprotected during accidental exposure (Source: ASCIA Guidelines: Acute Management of Anaphylaxis).
source_refs: ASCIA Guidelines: Acute Management of Anaphylaxis

options.text: Prescribe a 150 microgram adrenaline autoinjector and refer to allergy
options.rationale: Persistent vomiting with pallor and hypotonia after a food allergen is anaphylaxis, and the banded weight table assigns the 150 microgram device to children of 7.5 to 20 kg (Source: ASCIA Guidelines: Prescribing Adrenaline Autoinjectors; ASCIA Guidelines: Acute Management of Anaphylaxis).
source_refs: ASCIA Guidelines: Acute Management of Anaphylaxis

options.text: Advise strict egg avoidance with an oral antihistamine kept for reactions
options.rationale: Antihistamines treat urticaria but have no effect on airway or circulatory compromise, and relying on one after an anaphylactic reaction is a recognised contributor to fatal outcomes (Source: ASCIA Guidelines: Acute Management of Anaphylaxis).
source_refs: ASCIA Guidelines: Acute Management of Anaphylaxis

options.text: Arrange a supervised hospital egg challenge within the next two weeks
options.rationale: A challenge is used to confirm resolution of an allergy or to introduce a food of uncertain status, not to re expose a child weeks after a clear cut anaphylactic reaction (Source: ASCIA Guidelines: Prescribing Adrenaline Autoinjectors).

explanation.summary: Australian practice defines anaphylaxis by any acute onset illness with typical skin features plus respiratory, cardiovascular or persistent gastrointestinal involvement, and for food triggers repeated vomiting with pallor and hypotonia satisfies that definition. Device selection follows a banded weight table rather than per kilogram arithmetic, which is deliberate because caregivers must choose under pressure. Every child prescribed a device also needs a completed action plan, trainer device education and referral for confirmatory testing and a management plan. Egg allergy in infancy has a high rate of natural resolution, and most children can be re challenged in a supervised setting during the preschool years.
key_points: Persistent vomiting with pallor and hypotonia after a food is anaphylaxis
The 150 microgram device covers 7.5 to 20 kg and the 300 microgram device covers 20 kg and over
Do not compute the device dose from milligrams per kilogram
An antihistamine is never adequate treatment for anaphylaxis
Prescribe the device with an action plan and refer for specialist assessment
explanation.pearls: Baked egg in a cake or biscuit is tolerated by roughly seventy per cent of egg allergic children, and supervised introduction of baked egg is often the first step of the specialist plan rather than lifelong total avoidance.

sources.label: ASCIA Guidelines: Acute Management of Anaphylaxis

subtopic_detail: Disimpaction regimen for functional constipation with overflow soiling
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar in an outpatient clinic seeing a 4 year old boy. His parents report that for six months he has opened his bowels only every four or five days, passing hard pellets that hurt him, and that he hides behind the couch and crosses his legs when he needs to go. For the last month he has been leaving loose smears in his underpants several times a day, which his parents describe as diarrhoea and find very distressing.

He passed meconium on day one, has grown along the 50th centile and has a normal diet with adequate fluids. His abdomen is soft with a palpable indentable mass in the left iliac fossa. The spine, gluteal cleft, anal position and lower limb reflexes are all normal.

data_table.Examination: Palpable indentable faecal mass in the left iliac fossa, normal perianal appearance, normal lower limb neurology
data_table.Investigations: Growth on the 50th centile, no investigations performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Advise increased dietary fibre and fluids with review in one month
options.rationale: Dietary measures are part of long term maintenance but cannot clear an established faecal mass, and the overflow soiling will continue until disimpaction is achieved (Source: RCH CPG: Constipation).

options.text: Arrange an abdominal radiograph to confirm the degree of faecal loading
options.rationale: The diagnosis is clinical and radiographs correlate poorly with symptoms while adding radiation, so imaging is reserved for genuine diagnostic uncertainty (Source: RCH CPG: Constipation).

options.text: Give a phosphate enema now and start maintenance therapy from tomorrow
options.rationale: Rectal treatment is distressing at this age and reinforces withholding, so it is second line for children in whom an adequate oral macrogol regimen has already failed (Source: RCH CPG: Constipation).

options.text: Refer for anorectal manometry and a rectal suction biopsy of the bowel
options.rationale: Hirschsprung disease is suggested by delayed meconium passage, failure to thrive or an empty tight rectum, and none of those features is present in this well grown boy (Source: RCH CPG: Constipation).

options.text: Start an escalating oral macrogol regimen over up to seven days
options.rationale: Oral macrogol 3350 with electrolytes, escalated daily over three to seven days until the impaction clears, is first line disimpaction and is then continued as maintenance for months (Source: RCH CPG: Constipation; Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal).

explanation.summary: Overflow soiling is the commonest presentation of unrecognised functional constipation and is regularly misread by families as diarrhoea, so the palpable faecal mass and the withholding behaviour are the diagnostic anchors. Treatment has two distinct phases and the failures almost always come from skipping the first, because maintenance doses alone will not shift an established impaction. Maintenance must then run for at least several months and be weaned slowly, since early cessation reproduces the painful stool that started the withholding cycle. Toileting behaviour work with unhurried post meal sitting and a footstool is as important as the laxative itself.
key_points: Overflow soiling in a constipated child is not diarrhoea and does not need stool cultures
Disimpaction with escalating oral macrogol precedes maintenance dosing
Radiographs are not needed to diagnose functional constipation
Rectal treatments are second line after failed oral disimpaction
Maintenance continues for months with a slow wean
explanation.pearls: Red flags that move a constipated child out of the functional pathway are meconium passed after 48 hours, ribbon stools with an empty rectum, failure to thrive, and any abnormality of the lumbosacral spine or lower limb reflexes.

subtopic_detail: Excessive weight loss in an exclusively breastfed term newborn on day five
stem:
You are the resident on the postnatal domiciliary round seeing a 5 day old term girl born by normal vaginal birth at 39 weeks. Her birth weight was 3540 g and she weighs 3180 g today. Her mother is a first time parent who says the baby feeds about eight times in twenty four hours and comes off the breast quickly, and that her nipples are cracked and sore at the start of each feed.

The baby has had four heavy wet nappies and two yellow stools in the last day. She is alert between feeds, has moist mucous membranes and a soft fontanelle, and has no dysmorphic features. You watch a full feed and see a shallow latch with the baby taking only the nipple and clicking as she sucks. A serum bilirubin taken this morning sits well below the phototherapy threshold for her age.

data_table.Examination: Weight 3180 g representing a 10.2 per cent loss from birth weight, alert, moist mucous membranes, soft fontanelle
data_table.Investigations: Serum bilirubin well below the age specific phototherapy threshold, newborn screening sample already collected

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Admit her for nasogastric feeding and intravenous fluid rehydration
options.rationale: Admission for tube or intravenous feeding is reserved for a baby who is lethargic, clinically dehydrated, hypernatraemic or losing more than about twelve per cent, none of which describes this alert well perfused infant (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal Weight Loss and Dehydration).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Neonatal Weight Loss and Dehydration

options.text: Arrange lactation review with expressed milk top ups and reweigh daily
options.rationale: A loss of just over ten per cent in a well baby with a correctable shallow latch is managed by skilled feeding assessment, post feed expressed breast milk supplementation and daily weights until the trend turns (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal Weight Loss and Dehydration; Australian Breastfeeding Association clinical resources).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Neonatal Weight Loss and Dehydration

options.text: Reassure that this is expected and reweigh her at the six week check
options.rationale: Loss beyond ten per cent sits above the accepted physiological range and the cracked nipples with a shallow latch identify a mechanical problem that will worsen without intervention (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal Weight Loss and Dehydration).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Neonatal Weight Loss and Dehydration

options.text: Change to exclusive infant formula feeding and stop breastfeeding now
options.rationale: Abandoning breastfeeding for a correctable attachment problem forfeits the mother's stated goal and her supply, when supplementation alongside continued feeding achieves the same weight gain (Source: Australian Breastfeeding Association clinical resources).

options.text: Check serum bilirubin and start phototherapy while feeding continues
options.rationale: The bilirubin is already known and sits below the treatment line, so repeating it now does not address the feeding problem driving the weight loss (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal Jaundice).

explanation.summary: Term newborns lose weight for the first three to four days and normally regain birth weight by day ten to fourteen, with loss beyond ten per cent marking the point at which feeding needs formal assessment. The most common reversible cause is poor attachment, and observing an entire feed is more informative than any laboratory test. Supplementation with expressed breast milk protects supply because the breast is still being stimulated, whereas moving straight to formula reduces demand and often ends breastfeeding altogether. Serum sodium is the test that separates the well baby with mild dehydration from the infant heading toward hypernatraemic dehydration and its seizure risk.
key_points: Loss above ten per cent of birth weight requires assessment rather than reassurance
Watch a complete feed before making any management decision
Cracked nipples and clicking indicate a shallow latch amenable to repositioning
Expressed breast milk supplementation preserves supply
Escalate to admission for lethargy, poor perfusion, hypernatraemia or loss above twelve per cent
explanation.pearls: A serum sodium above 150 mmol/L in a breastfed newborn signals hypernatraemic dehydration, and correction must be slow at no more than 0.5 mmol/L per hour to avoid cerebral oedema.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Neonatal Weight Loss and Dehydration

subtopic_detail: Short stature with falling growth velocity despite a delayed bone age
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar seeing a 12 year old boy referred because he is the shortest in his class and is being teased about it. His height is on the 3rd centile and his weight on the 10th. Serial school measurements show he was on the 25th centile at age 9 and has crossed downward since, with a height velocity of 3 cm per year over the last two years.

His father says he himself did not shave until he was seventeen and grew after school finished. The boy eats well and reports no abdominal pain or altered bowels, and he plays soccer without limitation. His testicular volume is 3 mL bilaterally with no pubic hair, and a bone age radiograph is reported as delayed by two and a half years. His examination is otherwise normal with no dysmorphic features and a normal visual field to confrontation.

data_table.Examination: Height on the 3rd centile, weight on the 10th centile, mid parental height on the 50th centile, testicular volume 3 mL bilaterally
data_table.Investigations: Bone age delayed by two and a half years, height velocity 3 cm per year, no blood tests performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Reassure the family and reassess the height velocity in twelve months
options.rationale: Constitutional delay maintains a normal height velocity along a lower centile, whereas crossing centiles at 3 cm per year is pathological and another year of observation loses growth potential (Source: RCH CPG: Short Stature).

options.text: Refer for growth hormone stimulation testing at the endocrine clinic
options.rationale: Provocative growth hormone testing sits late in the pathway and is only interpretable once systemic disease, hypothyroidism and malabsorption have been excluded first (Source: RCH CPG: Short Stature).

options.text: Request a karyotype and pituitary magnetic resonance imaging scan now
options.rationale: Karyotype is directed at girls with possible Turner syndrome, and pituitary imaging follows biochemical evidence of deficiency or neurological signs rather than preceding basic screening (Source: RCH CPG: Short Stature).

options.text: Request coeliac serology, thyroid function and biochemical screening
options.rationale: Coeliac disease, hypothyroidism, renal impairment and inflammatory bowel disease all present with isolated growth failure and no gastrointestinal symptoms, so first line screening is transglutaminase with total immunoglobulin A, thyroid function, full blood count, electrolytes, inflammatory markers and insulin like growth factor 1 (Source: RCH CPG: Short Stature; Coeliac Australia clinical guidance).

options.text: Start testosterone priming to induce puberty and reassess in six months
options.rationale: Short course testosterone is used in constitutional delay to relieve psychosocial distress once pathology is excluded, and giving it now would mask the underlying cause while advancing the bone age (Source: RCH CPG: Short Stature).

explanation.summary: The single most useful growth parameter is height velocity, because a child on a low centile who is growing normally is usually constitutionally short or delayed, while a child crossing centiles has a disease process regardless of where they sit. A delayed bone age is not itself reassuring, since it accompanies constitutional delay, hypothyroidism, coeliac disease and growth hormone deficiency alike. Coeliac disease deserves particular attention because up to a third of affected children have no gastrointestinal symptoms and growth failure may be the only sign. Establishing the cause before intervening matters because treating the underlying disease often restores catch up growth without endocrine therapy.
key_points: Height velocity discriminates constitutional variants from pathology better than absolute height
Crossing downward through centiles after age 3 always requires investigation
A delayed bone age is common to both benign and pathological causes
Coeliac disease frequently presents with growth failure and no bowel symptoms
Screen for systemic disease before growth hormone testing or hormonal priming
explanation.pearls: Always request total immunoglobulin A alongside tissue transglutaminase antibodies, because selective immunoglobulin A deficiency occurs in about one in forty children with coeliac disease and produces a falsely negative serology.
